title: How Do Push Notifications Actually Work?
sources: Apple Technical Note TN2265 'Troubleshooting Push Notifications' (developer.apple.com): iOS 'attempts to establish a persistent network connection to the push service that will be shared by all push-capable apps on the system'
Apple Platform Deployment, 'Configure devices to work with APNs' (support.apple.com): APNs maintains persistent communication with Apple devices (TCP 5223, 443 fallback)

Android Developers, 'Optimize server-initiated actions' (developer.android.com): polling 'can waste network connection and power ... only to receive an answer that no new data is available'; FCM 'reduces the total number of network connections needed on a device' and lets the radio sleep more

Knock, 'How push notifications work on Apple and Android': the app or its servers don't deliver pushes themselves; the server sends the request with the target device token to APNs / FCM, which deliver it
Wikipedia, 'Apple Push Notification service': launched with iPhone OS 3.0 on June 17, 2009

lines.text: How does your phone know you got a message,
lines.caps: HOW DOES YOUR *PHONE | *KNOW | YOU GOT A *MESSAGE

lines.text: even when the app is closed?
You'd think every app keeps checking its own server,
but that would drain your battery fast.
Instead, your phone keeps one line open,
to Apple or Google, shared by all your apps.
When your friend texts you, the app's server
hands it to Apple or Google with your phone's token,
lines.caps: *HANDS IT | TO APPLE OR *GOOGLE | WITH YOUR *PHONE'S | *TOKEN

lines.text: and they push it down that open line.
Apple switched this on for iPhones in two thousand nine.
the app never actually talks to your phone,
Apple or Google deliver every buzz.
That ping isn't from the app, it's from a line that never hangs up.
lines.caps: THAT *PING | *ISN'T FROM | THE *APP | IT'S FROM A *LINE | THAT *NEVER | HANGS *UP
